881: A is correct because raising the CloudFront default TTL from 0 to 2 minutes lets CloudFront cache the static content at edge locations, improving performance while ensuring cached objects expire within about 2 minutes so stale content is not served for more than a few minutes. E is correct because a Cache-Control max-age directive of 24 hours allows CloudFront to cache objects for maximum performance, and creating a CloudFront invalidation on deployment immediately purges changed files from all edge caches so users get fresh content right after each release. Together these settings provide effective caching plus a deterministic way to eliminate stale content after deployments.
882: C is correct because a Compute Savings Plan provides discounted rates that automatically apply to both Amazon EC2 and AWS Lambda usage (as well as Fargate) for the 1-year commitment, giving cost coverage as the number of Lambda functions grows. Connecting the Lambda functions to the private subnets that contain the EC2 instances gives them direct network access to those instances through the VPC. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan would only discount the EC2 instances and not the increasing Lambda usage, and placing the functions in public subnets or leaving them in the Lambda service VPC would not provide the required direct private connectivity.
883: B is correct because AWS Budgets lets the company define a budget for each developer account and generate alerts on both actual and forecasted spend, so developers are notified when they exceed or are approaching their limit. AWS Budgets actions can then automatically apply a DenyAll IAM policy to the developer's role once the budget is reached, stopping further resource launches without any custom code or manual intervention. The other options depend on manual tagging with custom Lambda termination, daily report monitoring, or scheduled start/stop scripts, all of which carry more ongoing operational overhead.
884: A is correct because the web tier security group should only accept inbound HTTPS from the ALB's security group, ensuring web instances receive traffic solely through the load balancer. C is correct because the database tier should only accept inbound Microsoft SQL Server traffic (port 1433) from the application tier's security group, so only the business-logic tier can reach the database. E is correct because the application tier should only accept inbound HTTPS from the web tier's security group, maintaining strict tier-to-tier segmentation. Together these reference-based inbound rules enforce least-privilege, defense-in-depth communication for the three-tier architecture.
885: C is correct because a SageMaker Savings Plan covers the SageMaker portion of the workload at a discounted committed rate. D is correct because a single Compute Savings Plan automatically applies to Lambda, Fargate, and Amazon EC2 usage regardless of instance family, size, Region, or tenancy. With just these two plans the company covers all four services with the fewest purchases, whereas an EC2 Instance Savings Plan applies only to EC2 and cannot cover Fargate or SageMaker, and a Compute Savings Plan scoped to EC2, Lambda, and SageMaker would leave Fargate uncovered.
886: B is correct because Babelfish on Aurora PostgreSQL understands Microsoft SQL Server's T-SQL dialect, allowing the existing applications to run their SQL queries against Aurora PostgreSQL with little or no code modification. C is correct because the AWS Schema Conversion Tool converts the SQL Server schema and database objects to PostgreSQL while AWS Database Migration Service migrates the data into the new Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. This combination addresses both the schema and data migration and the query-language compatibility, enabling the migration with minimal application changes.
887: A is correct because enabling the EBS encryption-by-default account attribute (always encrypt new EBS volumes) automatically encrypts every newly created EBS volume with a KMS key, which both ensures encryption by default and prevents unencrypted EBS volumes from being created in the account. The other options either only detect already-noncompliant volumes after creation or are unrelated to enforcing encryption at volume creation time.
888: A is correct because Amazon Kinesis Data Streams in on-demand mode automatically provisions and scales capacity to absorb the fluctuating clickstream traffic throughout the day without manual shard management, and AWS Lambda can consume the stream records for real-time processing and analysis. Kinesis Data Firehose is built for batching and delivering data to destinations rather than custom real-time processing, Kinesis Video Streams is for video media, and Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink is a stream-processing engine rather than a scalable ingestion layer for capturing clickstream events.
889: B is correct because Amazon S3 Storage Lens provides organization-wide visibility across Regions into bucket configurations and activity, including versioning status, so the company can identify all S3 buckets that are not versioning-enabled from a single dashboard. CloudTrail captures individual API events rather than inventorying bucket configurations, IAM Access Analyzer for S3 detects buckets shared with external accounts, and Multi-Region Access Points are for routing requests rather than auditing configuration.
890: A is correct because S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval combines archive-tier storage pricing with millisecond retrieval latency, so files that must remain immediately accessible but are rarely accessed after the first 30 days can still be served directly without a restore step. Transitioning objects 30 days after creation matches the observed access pattern, and lifecycle expiration 4 years after creation satisfies the retention requirement. S3 One Zone-IA reduces durability which is risky for files that cannot be recreated, S3 Standard-IA has higher storage costs than Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarely accessed data, and option D delays deletion and adds unnecessary archive costs after the 4-year mark.
891: D is correct because S3 Multi-Region Access Points with a single global endpoint automatically route each user's request to the nearest S3 bucket over the AWS private network backbone, avoiding public internet congestion. An active-active configuration with S3 Cross-Region Replication keeps the regional buckets synchronized, and Multi-Region Access Points provide managed failover with minimal management, meeting both requirements. Using regional endpoints per Region would not provide automatic failover, and a replication rule alone does not solve traffic routing.
892: A is correct because an Auto Scaling group with a minimum and maximum of one keeps exactly one instance running for each legacy application and automatically launches a replacement from the pre-created AMI if the instance fails, achieving reliability and fault tolerance without changing the application design. The Application Load Balancer in front of the group provides a stable endpoint and health checks that trigger the automatic replacement. Running duplicate copies of a stateful legacy server risks conflicts, and backup-restore or refactoring approaches either extend recovery time or require the design changes that are not allowed.
893: A is correct because AWS Control Tower automatically provisions accounts with built-in guardrails that enforce security controls across the organization, and its recommended shared-networking pattern lets a central networking account own a VPC with public and private subnets. AWS RAM shares those subnets with the workload accounts so networking is centrally managed without duplicating infrastructure in every account. AWS Organizations alone does not apply automatic security guardrails, and routing every workload VPC through an inspection VPC with transit gateway attachments adds administrative overhead.
894: A is correct because hosting the static website in an Amazon S3 bucket is the most cost-effective, fully managed option and scales automatically as traffic increases, while a CloudFront distribution caches the content at edge locations to reduce origin load and further cut hosting costs. ElastiCache is an in-memory cache rather than a website-serving layer, and the Amplify-based options misuse ALBs and EC2 caching for static hosting.
895: D is correct because Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed native Windows file system that provides standard SMB protocol access, so the media application's servers can connect with no infrastructure to build, patch, or maintain. This delivers the least administrative overhead. A self-managed Windows file share on EC2 requires ongoing administration, and Storage Gateway volume or tape gateways are designed for hybrid on-premises integration with S3 rather than a managed AWS-native SMB file share.
896: B is correct because converting the cluster to an Aurora global database and configuring managed failover provisions a cross-Region secondary cluster in us-west-1 that replicates with a typical RPO of about 1 second, and managed failover typically completes in well under the 20-minute RTO target. Aurora global database also minimizes configuration changes because failover is managed automatically rather than through manual promotion and endpoint reconfiguration. A manual read replica, a separate cross-Region cluster, or DMS-based syncing all require more manual intervention to fail over.
897: A is correct because an AWS Fargate task runs a fully managed, serverless container that can execute a stateful job for an hour or longer without interruption risk, and Amazon EventBridge Scheduler reliably triggers the task on a cron schedule before the work week. AWS Lambda has a 15-minute execution limit that the job would exceed, Spot Instances can be interrupted which the job cannot tolerate, and AWS DataSync is a data-transfer service rather than a job-execution platform.
898: C is correct because Amazon Security Lake is a purpose-built, fully managed service that automatically centralizes security logs and findings from AWS and third-party sources into a customer-owned S3 data lake in a standardized format, enabling company-wide security assessment and improved workload protection. The alternatives require building custom data lakes, writing ingestion code, or configuring replication pipelines, which all involve far more development effort.
899: D is correct because a transit gateway acts as a central network hub with attachments for each application VPC and the shared services VPC, providing any-to-any routing so every application can reach the shared services VPC and each other. This hub-and-spoke model scales to more than 100 additional applications with minimal incremental administration, meeting the requirement of least administrative overhead. VPC peering is non-transitive and would require a rapidly growing full mesh of connections, and software VPN tunnels and Direct Connect are not suited to scalable VPC-to-VPC connectivity.
900: A is correct because a single ECS cluster can manage new cloud application containers with the AWS Fargate launch type while Amazon ECS Anywhere with the external launch type registers and runs the on-premises containers under the same managed control plane, satisfying the hybrid requirement. B is correct because an Application Load Balancer is the layer-7 load balancer that routes HTTP traffic to the cloud ECS services. Fargate cannot run on premises and ECS Anywhere does not support a Fargate launch type, so those alternatives violate the hybrid constraint, and a Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and is not intended for HTTP traffic routing.
